name: italian tomato white beans
instructions:
The maximalist italian tomato-and-cheese white bean skillet with a ratatouille-style eggplant tian on top. Built on Alison Roman's cheesy white bean tomato bake (NYT Cooking) with a set of additions that push the dish further into rich-italian-comfort territory: fresh garlic + onion powder in the base, heavy cream stirred in with the beans, RAW SLICED EGGPLANT ARRANGED IN A TIAN ON TOP OF THE BEANS (steamed through during a covered bake — see notes), cheese and breadcrumbs gratined over the eggplant, fresh parsley garnish. Related but distinct from italian-no-tomato-white-beans (see sibling note).

INGREDIENTS (4 servings):
- 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 3 fat garlic cloves, thinly sliced (fresh — see notes)
- 1-2 tsp onion powder
- 3 tbsp tomato paste
- 2 (15-oz) cans white beans (cannellini or great northern), drained and rinsed
- 1/2 cup boiling water
- ~1/2 cup heavy whipping cream (load-bearing — see notes on why the cream is the steam liquid for the eggplant)
- salt and black pepper
- 1 medium eggplant, sliced into 1/4-inch rounds (raw — cooks in the oven during the covered bake, see notes)
- 1/3 lb mozzarella or monterrey jack, coarsely grated (~1 1/3 cups)
- plain breadcrumbs (generous scatter for the gratin top — spray with oil, see notes)
- fresh parsley, chopped, for garnish

PROCEDURE:
1. HEAT OVEN TO 475°F.
2. In a 10-inch ovenproof skillet, heat the olive oil over medium-high. Fry the sliced fresh garlic until lightly golden (~1 min). Add the onion powder and stir briefly.
3. FRY THE TOMATO PASTE: stir in the tomato paste (watch for splatter) and fry ~30 seconds, reducing heat as needed to prevent the garlic from burning. This is the load-bearing flavor step — see notes.
4. Add the drained beans, boiling water, and generous pinches of salt and pepper. Stir to combine.
5. STIR IN THE CREAM: pour in the heavy cream and stir until the beans are coated in a loose tomato-cream sauce. Make sure there's enough liquid overall to steam the eggplant on top — add more cream or a splash of extra water if the bean base looks dry (see notes).
6. TIAN THE EGGPLANT ON TOP: arrange the raw eggplant rounds in overlapping shingled circles across the top of the beans (like a ratatouille tian). The eggplant sits on the beans, not folded in.
7. Top the eggplant with the grated cheese, then scatter breadcrumbs generously across the cheese. Spray the breadcrumbs with cooking spray (Pam or equivalent) for an even oil coat that crisps under the broiler.
8. COVERED BAKE — STEAM THE EGGPLANT: cover the skillet with a lid or aluminum foil and bake at 475°F until the eggplant is tender all the way through (~20-25 min). Steam from the cream + tomato-cream base cooks the eggplant while the cover traps moisture.
9. UNCOVER + GRATIN: remove the cover and bake another 5-10 min until the cheese has melted and the breadcrumbs are deeply golden.
10. OPTIONAL FINISHING BROIL: for extra char, run the skillet under the broiler 1-2 min. Watch closely — breadcrumbs go from golden to burnt fast.
11. GARNISH: scatter chopped fresh parsley across the top before serving. Serve at once with bread and a bitter-green salad.
notes:
=== ORIGIN + WHY THIS EXISTS ===

Started as Alison Roman's cheesy white bean tomato bake (NYT Cooking) — a spare 7-ingredient skillet-to-oven dish built on fried tomato paste + mozzarella. This version keeps her load-bearing techniques (fried tomato paste, high oven temp, cheese melted and browned in spots) but layers on additional ingredients that push the dish further into rich-italian-comfort territory. Roman's version reads clean and minimalist; this version reads maximalist and dinner-party. Both are valid; this one is the version I actually want to eat.

Additions vs. Roman's original: fresh garlic remains + onion powder added; heavy cream stirred in with the beans; breadcrumbs gratined ALONGSIDE the mozzarella (not instead of); raw eggplant sliced and arranged in a tian on top of the beans (steamed through during a covered bake, not pre-cooked); fresh parsley garnish.

=== ALISON ROMAN'S HEADNOTE (WHY THE BASE RECIPE EXISTS) ===

Roman's framing: this dish is 'for those of you who love lasagna's edges, where sticky tomato meets crisp cheese — even the middle.' The whole recipe is engineered to maximize the sticky-tomato-meets-crisp-cheese texture across every bite, not just the corners. The tube of tomato paste substitutes for the deep flavor of sun-dried tomato; frying it caramelizes the sugars and saturates the olive oil, giving you a mixture that glues onto everything you stir through it.

=== THE LOAD-BEARING TECHNIQUE — FRYING THE TOMATO PASTE ===

FRY THE TOMATO PASTE IN THE HOT GARLICKY OIL FOR 30 SECONDS: this is the whole trick. Raw tomato paste stirred into a dish stays flat and one-note. Fried tomato paste (30-60 sec in hot oil) caramelizes the natural sugars, drives off residual water, and dissolves into the oil as a concentrated red-orange coating — that oil now carries deep, almost sun-dried-tomato-adjacent flavor into anything you add next.

Don't skip and don't shortcut. Two failure modes:
- STIRRING TOMATO PASTE IN WITH THE BEANS/WATER: gives you a thin, unfried tomato-water base. The dish reads flat.
- FRYING TOO LONG / BURNING: tomato paste burns fast once the sugars caramelize past the sweet spot. Watch for the color to deepen from bright red to a rusty brick red; that's the finish line. Beyond that it goes bitter fast. Reduce heat as needed to keep the garlic from burning while the paste fries.

=== BOILING WATER, NOT COLD WATER ===

ADD BOILING WATER, NOT ROOM-TEMP OR COLD: cold water hitting the hot skillet drops the pan's temperature significantly and risks the caramelized tomato paste re-hydrating in a cooled pan (losing some of its concentrated character). Boiling water keeps the pan hot and lets the tomato-paste + oil + water blend into a loose sauce immediately. Have the kettle already boiling before you start frying the garlic.

=== FRESH GARLIC + ONION POWDER — BOTH ALLIUMS ===

Fresh sliced garlic stays from Roman's original. Onion powder is a personal addition — it goes into the base after the garlic browns and gives a background sweet-savory allium depth that fresh onion alone wouldn't deliver in the timescale this dish runs on. Onion powder is quicker than diced onion (which would need real sauté time to soften) and reads more even in the finished dish. Fresh diced onion would also work if you have the time; both are valid.

=== HEAVY CREAM — LOAD-BEARING FOR FLAVOR AND AS THE EGGPLANT STEAM LIQUID ===

Heavy cream (~1/2 cup) does two jobs here, both structural:

1. FLAVOR: stirred in with the beans and boiling water, it gives you a loose tomato-cream sauce that coats the beans rather than the thin tomato-water base Roman's original produces. Deliberate shift toward rich-italian-comfort territory — think tomato-cream pasta sauce logic, not spare-italian-technique logic.

2. STEAM LIQUID FOR THE EGGPLANT TIAN: the raw eggplant on top gets steamed through during the covered bake. That steam has to come from somewhere, and the cream + tomato base is the moisture reservoir. If the bean base looks dry when you're about to add the eggplant, add MORE CREAM (not just water) — cream evaporates more slowly than water and steams more effectively, plus it keeps the flavor register consistent. This is why cream isn't optional here the way it might feel like it should be.

Make sure there's visible liquid in the bean base before the eggplant tian goes on top. If not: extra splash of cream or a bit of water. A dry base means the eggplant doesn't cook through and the top of the pan burns while the eggplant stays firm.

=== MOZZARELLA + BREADCRUMBS BOTH ON TOP ===

Mozzarella melts into a stretchy sticky cheese blanket; breadcrumbs sprinkled on top of the cheese give you a crunchy gratin layer that Roman's version doesn't have. Both together read as an assembled italian-comfort-baked-thing (baked ziti / lasagna edge territory) rather than a spare bean bake.

MONTERREY JACK WORKS JUST AS WELL AS MOZZARELLA: monterrey jack is a fully valid substitute for the mozzarella here. It melts similarly (soft, stretchy, browns in spots), reads only slightly less italian-specific, and is often easier to have around than fresh mozzarella. Reach for whichever is in the fridge — no real quality gap. Both stay primary.

PARMESAN IS UNDERWHELMING HERE (SECONDARY): parmesan doesn't melt into a stretchy cheese blanket the way mozzarella / monterrey jack do, so it doesn't do the same top-of-dish work — reads flatter here than in the no-tomato sibling where it's the right cheese. Fine as a table finish or a supplementary grate, but not the main cheese slot.

SPRAY THE BREADCRUMBS WITH COOKING SPRAY: same technique as the frittata's breadcrumb gratin. Pam or equivalent, sprayed directly on the scattered breadcrumbs, gives an even oil coat that crisps under the high oven heat. Drizzling olive oil from a bottle always ends up patchy — the spray solves this cleanly.

=== EGGPLANT TIAN ON TOP (LIKE A RATATOUILLE) — RAW, STEAMED DURING COVERED BAKE ===

Eggplant is variant-specific — it belongs HERE, in the tomato variant, and NOT in italian-no-tomato-white-beans. Eggplant + tomato + cream + cheese is a classical italian combination (think parmigiana); eggplant + cream-only (no tomato) reads muddy and doesn't have the same lift.

ARRANGE RAW EGGPLANT IN A TIAN PATTERN ON TOP OF THE BEANS (not folded in): slice the eggplant into 1/4-inch rounds and shingle them in overlapping concentric circles across the top of the tomato-cream-bean base. Same technique as a ratatouille tian. The eggplant goes on top of the bean base and under the cheese layer — three distinct layers.

COVERED BAKE STEAMS THE EGGPLANT THROUGH: cover the skillet with a lid or foil for the first 20-25 min at 475°F. The cover traps steam from the cream + tomato base and cooks the eggplant from above and below. This is the whole reason the eggplant can go on raw — no pre-cooking sauté or bake step needed. Uncover for the last 5-10 min to gratin the cheese and breadcrumbs.

WHY THIS BEATS THE PRE-COOK APPROACH: previous versions of this recipe had you pre-sauté or pre-bake the eggplant and fold it into the beans. That works but has downsides — extra step, extra pan, and the eggplant loses its distinct shape as a topping layer. The tian approach gives you visible arranged eggplant on top (better presentation), skips the pre-cook (one fewer pan), and lets the cream/tomato steam do the work.

ENOUGH LIQUID IS CRITICAL: this only works if there's enough liquid in the bean base to steam the eggplant through. See the heavy cream note above — if the base looks dry, add more cream before the eggplant goes on. A dry base means the eggplant stays firm and the top of the pan burns.

Salt the eggplant rounds lightly if you want (draws out a bit of moisture), but it's optional — the covered steam bake tenderizes the eggplant regardless.

=== FRESH PARSLEY OR BASIL GARNISH — NON-OPTIONAL, SAME RULE AS THE NO-TOMATO SIBLING ===

A generous scatter of chopped fresh parsley OR torn basil across the top after baking is what makes this feel finished rather than dumped-in-a-skillet. The bright green herbal note against the rich tomato-cream-cheese-eggplant base is what keeps the dish from reading one-note-heavy. Chop and scatter off heat, right before serving.

Same herb-choice rule as the no-tomato sibling (see italian-no-tomato-white-beans): parsley reads cleaner and more italian-classic; basil is richer and works especially well here because of the tomato base — the classical basil-and-tomato pairing lands strongly. Pick one, don't mix both.

=== FORMAT — SKILLET TO OVEN, ~35-40 MIN TOTAL ===

~5-10 min for the stovetop bean base, then 20-25 min covered oven bake to steam the eggplant, then 5-10 min uncovered gratin. Total: ~35-40 min. Longer than Roman's original because of the eggplant tian + covered-steam step, but no pre-cook pan required (raw eggplant goes straight on) — active work is still modest.

High oven temp (475°F) throughout — same as Roman's original. The covered stage protects the top from over-browning while the eggplant steams; the uncovered final stretch does the sticky-tomato-meets-crisp-cheese work Roman engineered. Don't lower to 400°F 'to be safe' — you'll get soft cheese and pale breadcrumbs at the end.

=== WHITE BEANS OR CHICKPEAS — BOTH WORK ===

Roman's original allows chickpeas as an alternative to white beans. Cannellini gives the softest creamiest bite; great northern is slightly firmer; chickpeas are the firmest and add a nuttier register. All three work with the tomato-cream + mozzarella base. Cannellini is the default italian-white-bean choice.

=== SERVING — BREAD AND A BITTER GREEN SALAD ===

Roman's pairing stays: bread (to sop the tomato-cream oil) and a bitter-green salad (arugula, radicchio, endives, chicory) to cut the richness. Follow both. This maximalist version is even richer than Roman's original, so the bitter greens are even more important.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- italian-no-tomato-white-beans: the sister recipe. Cream + garlic breadcrumbs + parsley/basil + pine nuts, no tomato, no cheese. Reach for that when you're already serving another italian tomato dish on the plate (having two tomato-forward dishes side by side reads redundant) or when you want a cleaner cream-and-herb axis without the tomato weight. Lemon / raisins / red chili flakes / pine nuts work better in the no-tomato version — they don't fit here.
- shakshuka: eggs-in-tomato-sauce cousin. Different protein, different tomato form (canned crushed, not paste), same skillet + oven finish + molten protein on top skeleton.
- lemony-shrimp-and-bean-stew: the seafood white-bean sibling (NYT Cooking). Same white-bean base, built as a shrimp + leeks + lemon-butter-stock one-pot meal instead of a tomato-and-cheese bake.
